title: Wife of slain man questions Taser finding in Williams Lake inquest
subtitle: Coroner's jury recommends all RCMP officers be trained to use stun gun
article: The wife of a man killed by an RCMP officer near Williams Lake, B.C., thinks all but one of the recommendations made by the coroner's jury looking into the case are good ideas.
Sara Lewis's husband, Donald Lewis, died of a single gunshot wound in a confrontation with Const. Cole Brewer near McLeese Lake, a rural area north of Williams Lake, on Aug. 13, 2006.
Lewis, who described her husband as a gentle man, said she's not sure about the jury's recommendation to train all RCMP officers to use the stun gun.
"Tasers scare me on one hand because first of all we've all seen that they can kill ... and they're not sure what they can do to the heart," she said after the jury released its recommendations.
Lewis was shot by Brewer after the officer responded to a woman's call about a suspicious man illegally camping on private property, the inquest heard.

Brewer got into a confrontation with Lewis and used his fists, baton and pepper spray, before shooting him once. Brewer said he handcuffed the injured Lewis to a tree while he went back to his car to radio for assistance. Lewis died while handcuffed to the tree.

After hearing from 21 witnesses over six days of testimony, the coroner's jury came back Monday evening with six recommendations, including: all police vehicles in areas with questionable radio reception be equipped with radio repeaters, and policies be amended to allow for a second RCMP officer to attend when a call comes from an area where backup is not immediately available.
"Availability of hand-held communication is critical in rural areas," said the jury report.

Lewis said the recommendations, like police cross-checking the registered owner of a vehicle with possible people of interest, could help prevent what happened to her husband in the future. But, she said, "Tasers aren't the answer I don't think."
"The recommendations don't answer anything really. We don't really know what happened, we have to rely on the honesty of Const. Brewer," said Lewis.
Brewer, 36, said that during a physical altercation with Lewis, the 43-year-old tried to grab his pistol, saying, "I'm going to f---ing kill you."
Brewer told the inquest he had to shoot Lewis in order to save his own life.
RCMP officials say they are reviewing what the coroner's jury recommended, but that doesn't go far enough for Lewis.
"I want to see what's going to change, what's going to happen. What's the RCMP going to do to change how they operate?"
Stun guns have come under greater scrutiny since the death of a man at Vancouver's international airport last fall after he was hit with an RCMP Taser.
A B.C. public inquiry is underway, looking first at the general use of Tasers by law enforcement and later, specifically, at the death of Robert Dziekanski at the airport last October.
Const. Annie Linteau, an RCMP spokeswoman, said from Vancouver that the Williams Lake jury's recommendations will be examined.
"We'll carefully review them and figure out what the next course of action should be."
Sarah Lewis was joined in the hearing room by Linda Bush, the mother of Ian Bush, a 22-year-old Houston, B.C., man who died after being shot by an RCMP officer.

Ian Bush died in October 2005 after being arrested outside the Houston arena for holding an open bottle of beer. He was shot during a struggle with an RCMP officer in a cell at the Houston detachment.
A coroner's inquest into Bush's death cleared Const. Paul Koester of wrongdoing.
Also attending the Lewis inquest was Delores Young, whose son Kevin St. Arnaud was shot in December 2004 while being chased by Mounties in Vanderhoof, about 100 kilometres west of Prince George, B.C.
St. Arnaud, 29, was not armed, but the RCMP officer involved was cleared of wrongdoing.
